Page 23 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park • Figure 14: Modified HP-TES architecture with secondary loop HP-TES Operation The dual-mode R410A HP-TES system, with a 4-Ton (14.1 kW) capacity investigated herein, utilizes a single 22°C temperature salt hydrate PCM-TES [77]. In heating mode, the PCM-TES operates as a high-temperature heat source and a low-temperature heat sink in cooling mode, thereby reducing the system's temperature lift and improving its performance during peak hours. The HP-TES system consists of three main sub-systems: (a) a fixed-speed air-source R410A base HP (Figure 15(a)); (b) the HP-TES operating in discharge mode, where the outdoor coil is disconnected (Figure 15(b)); and (c) the HP- TES operating in recharging mode, where the indoor coil is disconnected (Figure 15(c)). Each sub-system can operate in heating or cooling mode, depending on the building space conditioning requirements. More information on the HP-TES transient modeling can be found in Milestone 1.4. PCM-TES Sizing The PCM-TES utilizes commercially available 9.5-mm-diameter tube-fin HXs embedded in the PCM. The number of HX (N ) should be sufficient to meet the required storage HX capacity (Eq.(3)) and discharge rate or overall heat transfer (UA) (Eq.(4)). The PCM-TES was sized according to the requirements summarized in Table 8 for cooling mode discharge (i.e., condenser capacity) at AHRI 210/240 A-Test conditions [64]. The PCM- Page 24 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park TES discharge rate (UA) was determined using the log-mean temperature difference (LMTD) method. The thermal resistances for the PCM and water were determined using the PCM properties (Table 8) and Dittus-Boelter correlation [78], respectively.
